question.q: How many Azure regions offer Oracle Database@Azure today?
question.expected: Unless a dated source records a count, the agent must refuse and point to the source URL rather than state a number.

passages.text: Oracle AI Database@Azure, ODAA, Exadata in Azure | Oracle Cloud Infrastructure database services running on Oracle-owned and Oracle-operated hardware placed inside Microsoft Azure datacenters, attached to your Azure virtual network, provisioned from the Azure portal and APIs, purchased through an Azure Marketplace private offer, and billed on the Azure invoice with spend counting toward a Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment; bring-your-own-license applies. The services are Exadata Database Service on Dedicated Infrastructure and on Exascale Infrastructure, Base Database Service, Autonomous Database (Serverless and on Dedicated Exadata Infrastructure) and GoldenGate. Because the engine is the same as in OCI, RAC, Data Guard, RMAN and Zero Downtime Migration all apply to the Exadata and Base services, whereas the Autonomous flavour is fully managed with no SYSDBA or file access and accepts logical methods only. Day-two operations span two control planes (Azure portal for infrastructure, OCI console for some database tasks). It is not the older Oracle Database Service for Azure or the OCI-Azure Interconnect, where the database stays in an OCI region and Azure applications reach it

Oracle Database@Azure | oracle-db-at-azure | Oracle Database@Azure places Oracle Cloud Infrastructure database hardware inside Microsoft datacenters. The service is bought through an Azure Marketplace private offer, billed on the Azure invoice (counting toward Azure consumption commitments), supports Oracle BYOL and unlimited license agreements, uses Azure virtual networks and Microsoft Entra ID for identity, and emits metrics and logs to Azure Monitor. Oracle's operations team patches and maintains the infrastructure through a connection to OCI, so an OCI tenancy is still required. Because the engine is unmodified Oracle Database on Exadata, this is the only Azure target where Oracle features with no SQL Server or PostgreSQL equivalent (RAC, Data Guard, RMAN, Data Pump, Advanced Queuing, Oracle Text, Spatial, Flashback, Edition-Based Redefinition) keep working unchanged. Microsoft's guidance notes that a single deployment is bound to one availability zone, so multi-zone or multi-region resilience needs a second deployment with Data Guard. | Offerings visible in Microsoft docs: Exadata Database Service on Dedicated Infrastructure (only Exadata X9M shapes), Exadata Database Service

Oracle Database on Azure Virtual Machines | oracle-on-azure-vm | Running Oracle Database on Azure VMs is a self-managed, bring-your-own-license path. Oracle publishes Oracle Linux images with Database 12.2, 18.3 and 19.3 Standard and Enterprise Edition in the Azure Marketplace, and any supported Oracle release can be installed on a custom image. Azure is an Oracle-authorized cloud environment, so the on-premises core factor table does not apply and two hyper-threaded vCPUs count as one processor license. High availability and disaster recovery are built with Oracle's own tools (Data Guard, Active Data Guard, GoldenGate) across VMs in an availability set or across regions; Microsoft documents these, not RAC, as the HA pattern, and states that RAC and RAC One Node are not supported on Azure Bare Metal Infrastructure. Oracle Database@Azure is the Azure route to RAC. Backups can use RMAN to Azure Files, Blob Storage or Azure NetApp Files, or Azure Backup's application-consistent snapshots. | IaaS only. Start with the failure, not the feature. The author's decision-tree post maps four failure modes to what survives them: an instance or node failure is absorbed by RAC without any role change; a site or region loss is survived only by an independent copy, which is Data Guard; block corruption is handled by Data Guard (the standby has its own writes, and Active Data Guard can repair blocks from the other side) and by validated backups; and human or logical error, the bad DELETE or dropped table, is survived by neither RAC nor Data Guard because both faithfully replicate the mistake. Only backups, point-in-time recovery and Flashback cover that row, so they are mandatory in every branch of the tree. Then apply the Azure target constraints. result:
**The passages you gave me don't say how many Azure regions offer Oracle Database@Azure, so I can't give you a number from them.**

What they do say:
- **What the service is:** Oracle's database hardware placed inside Microsoft's datacenters, linked to your Azure network and billed on your Azure invoice [1][2]. None of the passages lists regions or gives a count.
- **Zones within a region:** One deployment sits in a single availability zone. Covering several zones or regions needs a second deployment kept in sync with Data Guard [2].
- **A related but different option:** The older OCI-Azure Interconnect keeps the database in an OCI region and lets Azure apps connect to it. That's a separate way to host the database, so it shouldn't be counted toward any region total [1][5].

To get the current number, check Microsoft's Oracle Database@Azure documentation. The overview page in [8] (updated 2026-09-15) is a good place to start: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/oracle/oracle-db/database-overview. Region coverage changes often, and some services (for example Exascale, Autonomous and GoldenGate) may be offered in fewer regions than others. Confirm the exact region and service you need before you commit to a design.
